newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian senators defy Yeltsin, send back art law.
newsitem.headline: Russian senators defy Yeltsin, send back art law.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, already at odds with parliament over issues as diverse as the national budget and the mummified body of Lenin, faced a new challenge on Tuesday, this time on art treasures seized from wartime Germany.

The upper chamber, usually less hostile to the Kremlin than the communist-dominated lower house, sent back to Yeltsin on Tuesday a bill which he has been refusing to sign because it would thwart his attempts to return the art to Germany.

Senators in the Federation Council voted overwhelmingly for a resolution rejecting Yeltsin's contention that there had been procedural irregularities when the bill was passed and sent the draft law back to the Kremlin for signing along with a letter accusing the president of "obviously exceeding his powers".

The chairman of the Federation Council's regulations committee, Valery Borodayev, said the chamber had found no irregularities in the law and that, in any case, such a decision was not for Yeltsin to take but the Constitutional Court -- once the president had signed the bill into law.

"Thus the President, having assumed the functions of the Constitutional Court and refusing to sign the law has over-reached his powers and failed to fulfill his constitutional duties," Borodayev said.

Council speaker Yegor Stroyev said parliament should take the president to the Constitutional Court if he again refused to sign the bill. The Council, comprised of governors and local assembly leaders from Russia's regions, was once full of Yeltsin appointees, but many lost their seats in elections last winter.

Deputy Culture Minister Mikhail Shvydkoi, an art expert who has documented Russia's hoard of "transferred valuables", told Ekho Moskvy radio the president was more likely to sign the bill and then take the issue to arbitration in the Constitutional Court than to persist in withholding his signature.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin had said already last month that Yeltsin was likely to refer to the Court.
But the president, who saw his original veto overturned by two-thirds majorities in both houses, preferred to send it back to parliament.
A Kremlin spokesman declined to comment on Tuesday.
The matter is the latest in a series of rows between the powerful presidency and relatively weak parliament.

The issue of the budget, where the State Duma lower house is stalling government spending cuts, is considerably more serious for the nation. Lenin's body, whose removal from its Red Square mausoleum Yeltsin suggested last week should be subject to a referendum, is more likely to stir passions at home.

But the trophy art bill is an embarrassment internationally for Yeltsin as he heads off next week for talks with fellow world leaders, including German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, at the Denver Group of Seven (G7) summit.

Yeltsin insists the bill is contrary to international law and hence to the Russian constitution. Under it, the return of every item of war booty would be subject to individual parliamentary approval, effectively blocking the handover.

Germany, Russia's biggest trading partner and creditor, wants Russia to return the art seized by Soviet troops at the end of World War Two. The vast hoard includes a rare Gutenberg bible, gold artefacts supposedly from the site of ancient Troy and paintings by Impressionists Claude Monet and Henri Matisse.
But many Russians say they should stay as compensation for destruction during the Nazi invasion and for the sufferings of the Soviet Union, which lost 27 million citizens in the war.
